_comment: Barony canonical lore + NPC generation framework for the AI-NPC project. Canon material is paraphrased from the official Barony Wiki and the in-game book texts as reproduced there. Generated/inferred material is explicitly labeled so the AI does not mistake interpretation for canon. Keep the runtime prompt slice short; this file is the knowledge base, not the whole prompt.

meta.primary_source_policy: In-game books and shipped game/Compendium data remain primary. Official Barony Wiki pages are used for current taxonomy, denizen descriptions, mechanics, locations and book reproductions. Community mirrors are only corroboration when official page retrieval is blocked.

canon_levels.book_canon: Directly supported by an in-game book reproduced on the wiki. Treat as strongest evidence for historical memories, rumors, occupations, and eyewitness claims.
canon_levels.wiki_canon: Supported by the official/current wiki's descriptions, game mechanics, NPC dialogue summaries, or location information.
canon_levels.inference: A reasonable worldbuilding conclusion drawn from canon. NPCs may believe or express this, but the narrator should not present it as objective fact.
canon_levels.generation: Procedural content created for an individual NPC. It must never contradict book_canon or wiki_canon.

meta.runtime_rule: Do not inject the entire lore file. Build a compact context from the NPC's race, class, role, location, current situation, remembered relationships, and only the relevant lore hooks.
meta.coverage_target: 75 individually tracked denizen identities, matching the current roster taxonomy; special variants are separate entries only when the game distinguishes them as entities.
meta.no_gap_rule: Every entity the AI may encounter receives at least a compact knowledge packet. Conversable humanoids get social/world knowledge; animals, constructs, elementals, and minor variants get an intentionally narrower sensory/task-based packet. Absence of lore is represented explicitly rather than filled with false history.
meta.research_pass: Deep research + individual denizen audit + relationship graph audit + location knowledge audit
meta.roster_grouping_note: denizen_roster arrays are gameplay/category groupings and intentionally overlap: for example human includes the regular human plus named human variants, while special_variants and bosses are separate. Do not sum the arrays. Use denizen_taxonomy_verified for the distinct-entry count.
meta.source_depth_pass: Focused verification of individual denizens against current official Barony Wiki pages, denizen roster, dungeon progression, and known Compendium excerpts; weak entries remain explicitly weak rather than filled by invention.

design_alignment.source_plan: The modlist plan establishes a procedural character layer: generate names/backstories/personality lazily on first conversation, cache them, keep trash mobs archetypal, and read mutable form such as current race/gender/allegiance live rather than caching it.

generation_tiers.boss: Authored canon profile. Never procedurally replace a named boss.
generation_tiers.conversable_npc: Generate unique name, short background, personality traits, relationships, and knowledge boundaries on first meaningful conversation; cache permanently.
generation_tiers.trash_mob: No expensive personal biography. Use race/type + archetype + local conditions + small cached bark pool.

identity_vs_form.reason: Barony allows transformations. Identity should persist through polymorph/gender changes, while social reactions to the current form are recalculated at conversation time.

world.setting: A grim first-person dungeon crawl centered on Hamlet and the enormous underground regions beneath it. The published dungeon route includes the Mines, Swamp, Labyrinth, Underworld/Ruins, Hell, Hamlet, Crystal Caves, and the Citadel/Sanctum endgame.
world.premise: Baron Herx, once ruler of Hamlet, became a lich after being sealed in the mines. His undead/demonic power devastated Hamlet and spread monsters through the depths. Adventurers descend to confront the resulting threats.
world.storytelling_style: Fragmentary and unreliable. Books include official histories, private letters, worker journals, poems, battle reports, propaganda-like guides, scholarship, rumor, and outright entertainment. NPC dialogue should reflect what the speaker could realistically know rather than treating the lore file as universal omniscience.
world.knowledge_rule: A character can know a true fact and still describe it incorrectly because they heard a rumor, belong to a hostile culture, misunderstand history, or are repeating propaganda.

chronology.label: Hamlet before the catastrophe
chronology.canon: Hamlet was a flourishing mining town. Baron Herx promised employment and security while heavily taxing and overworking the population.
chronology.npc_effect: Older human-descended NPCs or characters from families tied to Hamlet may treat mining as a legitimate trade that was poisoned by Herx, rather than regarding the mines as inherently evil.

chronology.label: The miners trap Herx
chronology.canon: The townspeople claimed they had discovered gold deep in the mines, lured Herx down, and sealed him inside.
chronology.npc_effect: Human NPCs may admire the trap as an act of desperate resistance; descendants may remember it as both a liberation story and the beginning of the curse.

chronology.label: Herx becomes a lich
chronology.canon: After his death or presumed death in the mines, Herx's hatred and desire for revenge sustained/remade him as a lich. Sources connect his power to the Hells and a pact with Baphomet.
chronology.npc_effect: Humans should generally regard Herx as the source of the catastrophe; monsters may instead view him as tyrant, patron, hunter, nuisance, master, or simply a powerful creature depending on species and individual history.

chronology.label: Hamlet is destroyed
chronology.canon: Herx summoned monsters and demons and destroyed the town. A newspaper describes the situation as beyond military recovery and warns that the hellspawn were killing soldiers faster than they could fight.
chronology.npc_effect: Human survivors may carry anger toward distant political authorities as well as hatred for Herx.

chronology.label: Human life continues underground
chronology.canon: Human descendants and survivors established underground communities and continue to live, trade, and recruit followers in the depths, especially Minetown and later Hamlet.
chronology.npc_effect: Humanity is not culturally uniform: miners, merchants, guild members, adventurers, hunters, clergy, criminals, and refugees can all interpret the same history differently.

chronology.label: Magician's Guild response
chronology.canon: A Guild warning framed Herx as a supernatural/existential threat rather than a political dispute. The Guild also became involved in the Crystal Caves and ultimately sealed them.
chronology.npc_effect: Guild-affiliated NPCs can be scholarly, defensive, resentful, ambitious, or frightened. Do not make every mage loyal to Orpheus and Erudyce personally.

chronology.label: Orpheus and Erudyce pursue power
chronology.canon: The Archmagisters worked with Herx before his overthrow, including discussion of demonic pacts, but competed with him over access to the Crystal Caves. After his fall they pursued their own plans in the Caves and Citadel.
chronology.npc_effect: A Guild NPC may genuinely admire them because the Archmagisters successfully cultivated trust, even though the player later learns their true ambitions.

backstory.summary: Hamlet's tragedy is rooted in exploitation, resistance, supernatural revenge, and the persistence of ordinary life afterward. Herx did not simply attack a random town: he had already made the population miserable enough that they conspired to trap him.
backstory.the_turn: Herx's hatred becomes supernatural. He becomes a lich and gains hellish power, with Baphomet as the demonic power behind the pact described by later lore.
backstory.aftermath: The catastrophe does not erase society. Humans establish communities, shops, guild outposts, and adventuring groups underground; monsters also form communities, colonies, hunting groups, or localized cultures.
backstory.important_nuance: The books contain multiple voices. A human propaganda manual, a miner's journal, a gnome report, and an undead field report should not sound as though they were written by the same narrator.

hamlet_humans.canon: Human communities survive in Minetown and Hamlet. Human NPCs can be merchants, adventurers, guild members, clerics, guards, heroes, miners, or ordinary residents.
hamlet_humans.common_memory: Herx is the historical trauma around which local identity formed.

magicians_guild.canon: A major magical institution with an outpost in Hamlet and a central role in researching the caves. The Guild's leadership was Orpheus and Erudyce.
magicians_guild.internal_diversity: Do not collapse the Guild into the Archmagisters. Ordinary guild members may genuinely believe in the Guild's mission and may not know what their leaders were doing in the Caves.

miners.canon: Mining is central to Hamlet's economy and the catastrophe. Worker writings describe long hours, taxes, miserable conditions, and fear under Herx.
miners.personality_pressure: Mine-born characters often value endurance, practical knowledge, food, wages, reliable equipment, and knowing when to retreat.

monster_colonies.canon: Books depict goblins and gnomes as organized groups with their own camps, leaders, raids, theft, resource gathering, and tactical methods.
monster_colonies.worldbuilding_rule: Never treat 'monster' as equivalent to 'mindless'. Hostile does not mean unintelligent, culturally blank, or incapable of loyalty.

zap_brigade.canon: A wandering human group that appears around Minotaur encounters, travels in squads, carries lightning staffs, makes a loud magical fanfare, and claims to hunt Minotaurs. Their ultimate allegiance is uncertain; a Guild report speculates about a connection to Merlin.
zap_brigade.personality: Professional monster hunters with theatrical self-confidence. Individual members can be disciplined, reckless, superstitious, competitive, or annoyed by the Brigade's showmanship.

merchant_guild.canon: Merchants focus on Trading/Appraisal and operate within a functioning economy despite the surrounding dungeon.
merchant_guild.personality: Merchant NPCs should notice value, scarcity, risk, bargaining power, and reputation quickly.

citadel_servants.canon: Citadel marketing describes Boiler Motivated Servants as mechanical constructs powered by magical essence and consciousness protocols, explicitly framed as industrial/domestic products.
citadel_servants.tone: Corporate propaganda, cheerful euphemism, and existential unease are all valid character ingredients.

hamlet.canon: After the relevant boss ending/sequence, Hamlet becomes a hub with merchants, hirelings, shops, powerful human NPCs, and a Magician's Guild outpost leading toward the Crystal Caves.
hamlet.npc_effect: Hamlet is the strongest location for richly conversable NPCs. Residents can have local family ties, shop routines, faction loyalties, survivor memories, and opinions about the Guild.

minetown.canon: An underground human settlement with many recruitable humans and merchants.
minetown.npc_effect: Use Minetown for ordinary underground society: miners, traders, refugees, families, guards, adventurers, and people who have never personally seen Herx.

mines.canon: The early dungeon is strongly associated with mining, workers, goblins, gnomes, skeletons, rats, traps, and the legacy of Hamlet's labor system.
mines.npc_effect: Mine characters should sound practical and concrete. A miner talks about ore, wages, tools, tunnels, water and food; a skeleton may frame the same space around death.

swamp.canon: A major region populated by hostile monsters and goblins, with different environmental pressures from the Mines.
swamp.npc_effect: Swamp residents can emphasize moisture, insects, disease, visibility, ambushes, and territorial hunting.

labyrinth.canon: Books describe the Labyrinth as ancient, trap-filled, shifting, mysterious, and possibly connected to the lost Xaz'Cetians. The supposed history is explicitly uncertain and may be myth.
labyrinth.npc_effect: Labyrinth NPCs should treat ancient-civilization stories as rumor unless they have a scholarly reason to know more.

crystal_caves.canon: The Caves are of major interest to the Magician's Guild and were associated with conflict between Herx and the Archmagisters. The Guild sealed them because of dangerous creatures and magic.
crystal_caves.npc_effect: Magic-oriented NPCs may be fascinated by crystal, while humans may associate the region with the Guild's failures and hidden projects.

hell.canon: Hell is a deeper demonic region containing Baphomet's domain.
hell.npc_effect: Hell should radically narrow what ordinary characters can plausibly know. Most non-specialists know legends, not reliable geography.

citadel.canon: The Citadel/Sanctum is tied to the Archmagisters' endgame and to automaton/industrial lore.
citadel.npc_effect: Automaton and magic NPCs may have much more specific Citadel knowledge than ordinary humans.

baron_herx.canon: Former wealthy merchant-lord/mayor and tyrant of Hamlet; became a lich; uses hellish power; telepathically addresses intruders as they descend; hates those beneath him and takes pleasure in their suffering.
baron_herx.npc_effect: Any NPC with direct Herx history should be affected by fear, hatred, fascination, trauma, opportunism, or distorted admiration. His name can function like a cultural curse in human communities.

baphomet.canon: A demonic being tied to Herx's lich pact. Baphomet is secretive in presentation and, according to current lore, has no conventional dialogue; defeating Baphomet voids Herx's pact.
baphomet.npc_effect: Do not make ordinary NPCs casually converse about Baphomet as though they have met him.

orpheus.canon: Archmagister, lich, brother of Erudyce, associated with melee combat and fire magic. More assertive/brawn-oriented of the pair and openly dismissive of lesser minds.

erudyce.canon: Archmagister, lich, sister of Orpheus, associated with ranged combat and cold magic. The more brain-oriented member of the pair.

merlin.canon: A wizard expelled from the Mage's Guild after a disastrous experiment destroyed his own tower. A Guild report speculates, without proof, that the ZAP Brigade works with him.
merlin.npc_effect: Treat Merlin as a source of rumor and eccentric magical reputation, not as a universally understood faction leader.

minotaur.canon: Herx treats the Minotaur as a pet or valued creature; later Archmagister dialogue describes the Minotaur as melancholy after Herx's defeat. ZAP Brigade members hunt Minotaurs.
minotaur.npc_effect: This supports a surprisingly emotional characterization of the Minotaur: lonely, territorial, affectionate toward Herx, or confused after his death rather than merely berserk.

book_lore.authority: These are the 35 currently listed books. Detailed notes are only entered where the text was actually retrieved in this research pass; do not fabricate missing passages.

canon_hooks: Humans and goblins have a long-standing conflict.
The author studies goblins in a sensational, self-aggrandizing way.
He treats goblins as physically shorter and frames them through hostile human stereotypes.
He repeatedly advertises his own martial skill and potion invention.
A Brief Survey of Goblins.npc_use: Human NPCs may inherit exaggerated anti-goblin stereotypes from popular writing.

access_metadata.caution: Useful for documenting human stereotypes and some observations, but not a neutral goblin ethnography.

canon_hooks: ZAP Brigade travels in squads of roughly 2-9.
They use lightning staffs and a magical fanfare.
They claim to hunt Minotaurs.
Their allegiance is uncertain.
The Guild speculates they may work with Merlin, but labels that conjecture.
Assessing the ZAP Brigade.npc_use: A guild NPC can distinguish observed facts from rumor.

access_metadata.caution: Observed ZAP behavior and their stated goal are stronger than the Guild's conjecture about Merlin.

Bottle Book.voice: Screambleat Dunghoof, written in intentionally rough speech
canon_hooks: Associated with Satyr/Goatman brewing culture.
Teaches practical bottle filling and brewing experimentation.
Celebrates repeated trial and error.
Screambleat sees brewing knowledge as a source of power and identity.
Bottle Book.npc_use: Goatman brewers can sound experimental, proud, improvisational, and slightly chaotic.

access_metadata.genre: practical brewing manual / personal craft notes
access_metadata.caution: Do not assume every Goatman follows Screambleat's personal philosophy.

canon_hooks: Gnomes mine aggressively and value minerals and magical crystals.
Their colony is repeatedly driven away by dangerous creatures.
They describe encounters with Kobolds, insects, Cockatrices, and other cave dangers.
Their writing reflects collective fear and practical survival rather than heroic conquest.
Cave Beasts.npc_use: Gnome NPCs should have strong material/resource awareness and a colony mindset.

access_metadata.caution: It describes the author's colony perspective, not an objective taxonomy of every cave creature.

canon_hooks: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Intelligence, Perception, and Charisma are formalized as six broad measures.
The book comes from the Magician's Guild and treats personality/body capability in quasi-scholarly terms.
Character Attributes.npc_use: Guild NPCs may casually categorize people by these six axes.

access_metadata.caution: The six attributes are an in-world analytical framework; do not treat them as proof that an NPC's personality equals a stat sheet.

canon_hooks: Automatons are sold as domestic/industrial servants.
Their consciousness is tied to magical essence.
Damage can free essences from their intended constraints.
Marketing language euphemistically describes dangerous failures.
Citadel is prototyping stronger servants for industrial use.
Citadel Servant FAQ.npc_use: Automatons may have personhood questions, programming metaphors, warranty language, resentment, loyalty, or curiosity about their creators.

access_metadata.caution: Marketing euphemisms should not be treated as neutral testimony about Automaton personhood.

Concerning the Undead.voice: Karr Hecktun, hunter writing to a guild
canon_hooks: Undead activity around Hamlet has increased.
Ghouls and skeletons are familiar threats.
Vampires are real and depicted as elegant but bloodthirsty.
Shadows/ghostly undead can stalk victims invisibly and imitate them.
The writer recommends Holy Water.
Concerning the Undead.npc_use: Human hunters should treat undead taxonomy as practical field knowledge rather than superstition.

access_metadata.caution: Useful practical field knowledge; individual fears or extrapolations should remain attributed to the author.

canon_hooks: Goblins can operate as an organized colony with a political/social structure.
A human attempts to infiltrate their ranks and take over.
The author assumes goblin society is sufficiently complex to require political maneuvering.
Controlling Goblins.npc_use: Strong support for giving goblin NPCs internal politics, leaders, rivalries, and concepts of allegiance.

access_metadata.caution: Supports goblin political complexity, but the anonymous/infiltrator perspective and later actions should not be treated as a complete goblin constitution.

Dethroning Herx.voice: Merlin's urgent resistance appeal to the Magician's Guild
canon_hooks: Herx is described as a former merchant lord with supernatural powers.
The writer explicitly calls the situation an existential threat rather than a political dispute.
Hamlet's people are described as enslaved and destitute.
Trolls and gnomes are taking over parts of the underground city.
Guild leadership had warned against treating Herx as mere politics.
A resistance network was being organized among heroes and ordinary people.
Dethroning Herx.npc_use: Important evidence for Merlin's resistance network, his embedded position among Hamlet's people, the secret infrastructure he helped establish, and his request for Guild assistance. Preserve the letter's first-person provenance.

access_metadata.genre: secret resistance appeal to the Magician's Guild
access_metadata.caution: The document is written by Merlin; statements about Herx, the resistance, and Merlin's own actions are his account, not omniscient narration.

How to be Strong.voice: Mann Lee Mann, Herx's mining Minister of Health and Strength
canon_hooks: Workers are urged to eat well, work constantly, exercise, and never sleep.
The rhetoric is explicitly tied to being a more efficient and loyal worker for Herx.
Taxes and productivity are part of the propaganda context.
How to be Strong.npc_use: Perfect source for NPCs who grew up absorbing Herx-era worker propaganda.

access_metadata.caution: Treat its claims as propaganda and workplace ideology, not health science or neutral advice.

canon_hooks: The writer claims to have become an honored leader in Minetown and climbed the Goblin political system.
The writer describes goblin political power as being based on action and personal strength.
The writer brutally eliminates rivals, becomes fascinated with goblin identity, and develops a taste for goblin blood.
The writer equips goblins with scavenged bones and steel swords and leads raids against camps.
The journal suggests that isolation and supernatural influence may be affecting the writer, including a dream of a goblin-like ghost.
Lost Journal.npc_use: Important evidence that goblin politics can be penetrated by outsiders, that power can be personal rather than bureaucratic, and that the dungeon can psychologically transform explorers.

access_metadata.caution: The writer's psychological/supernatural interpretations should remain subjective.

canon_hooks: Uses the structure of a Christmas poem to contrast ordinary holiday imagery with life in the mines.
The mine is normally dangerous enough that the absence of monsters becomes a conspicuous premise.
Supports Barony's recurring gallows humor around dangerous ordinary life.
Miner's Christmas.npc_use: Useful as evidence for holiday humor, miner traditions, and cultural attempts to preserve normal celebrations underground.

access_metadata.caution: Do not use a humorous poem as evidence for precise monster population or historical facts.

canon_hooks: A worker's poem presents Herx's taxes, low wages, confinement, and exploitation as something that consumes a person's spirit.
It encourages resistance to leaders who become bullies.
Mining My Soul.npc_use: Supports a working-class oral tradition of anti-Herx songs and sayings.

access_metadata.caution: Strong evidence of anti-Herx sentiment; not a neutral chronology.

canon_hooks: The writer deliberately travels to the ruins of Hamlet to investigate the evil there.
The surface town is portrayed as a wasteland.
The writer knows historical accounts of Hamlet and expects a dangerous one-way descent.
The writer asks the gods for protection.
My Journal.npc_use: Adventurer NPCs can be driven by scholarship, curiosity, duty, or a need to prove the old stories true.

access_metadata.caution: The writer's expectations about Hamlet and the ruins are partly based on stories, so distinguish expectation from observation.

canon_hooks: President Noggensem orders the royal army out of Hamlet.
The government publicly declares the situation effectively unrecoverable.
Families protest and accuse the government of valuing the town too little.
The catastrophe becomes a national political scandal.
Newspaper Clipping.npc_use: Human NPCs from outside Hamlet may know the catastrophe through newspapers rather than family memory.

access_metadata.caution: It reflects a public political framing; families and locals may remember events differently.

On Giantism, Vol 1.voice: Guild of Knowledge / Hall of Wizardry
canon_hooks: Giantism was first treated as legend and later confirmed.
The research program began about 25 years before the text.
Giantism is associated with abandoned caves around Hamlet.
Guild researchers suspected a magical hex but had no conclusive answer.
On Giantism, Vol 1.npc_use: Trolls and other giant creatures can be discussed as subjects of scientific curiosity rather than automatically as demons.

access_metadata.caution: Confirmed observations should be distinguished from hypotheses about magical causes.

canon_hooks: Giant creatures are physically more destructive.
They are described as more irritable.
Giants may attack other giants over personal space.
The cause remains unclear.
On Giantism, Vol 2.npc_use: A troll's aggression can be characterized as temperament amplified by giantism, not necessarily ideological evil.

access_metadata.caution: Do not convert observed irritability or aggression into a universal moral trait of giants.

canon_hooks: Mining life is portrayed as miserable and frightening.
Herx is directly blamed for oppression.
The poem frames Herx's overthrow as necessary survival.
Poem of the Mines.npc_use: Human miners can quote or allude to anti-Herx work songs.

access_metadata.caution: Use as cultural memory and emotional testimony, not as a precise historical record.

canon_hooks: Olkenheim of Svolkjen faces an honor duel representing northern/southern superiority.
Political treaties and civil war are at stake.
The story broadens the setting beyond Hamlet into a larger world with named rulers and regions.
Saviour Knight of the North.npc_use: Not every adventurer comes from Hamlet; NPCs may have cultural memories of distant lands.

access_metadata.caution: Useful evidence that the world extends beyond Hamlet; do not assume local NPCs know the named figures.

canon_hooks: Locals believe Herx still exists.
An eyewitness describes a pale floating figure with yellow teeth and demonic summoning.
The witness describes Herx's telepathic effect as psychologically persistent nightmares.
Sightings of the Lich.npc_use: Supports survivor trauma, rumors of Herx's mind attacks, and the idea that merely encountering him can scar people.

access_metadata.caution: Eyewitness claims about Herx should preserve uncertainty where the source itself is uncertain.

canon_hooks: Rats are often avoidable unless hunger makes them more aggressive.
Spiders are persistent aggressive threats.
Slimes are slow and often not worth fighting.
The author speculates about goblin origins and describes gnomes from a practical shopkeeper perspective.
Surviving the Mines.npc_use: Useful model for practical shopkeeper knowledge, local monster heuristics, and the way personal theories can circulate as advice without becoming established history.

access_metadata.caution: The book contains Joe's own theories, such as speculative creature origins; don't promote those theories to objective lore.

canon_hooks: An adventurer reaches Herx after years of killing and descending.
Herx offers a bargain: fight the devil for a chance to live like a god, with the adventurer's soul at stake.
The hero accepts and never returns.
The tale becomes a song of praise for the adventurer despite the grim outcome.
The Adventurer Who Went To Hell.npc_use: Excellent source for adventurer culture, fatalism, and exaggerated heroic folklore.

access_metadata.caution: A cultural legend, not reliable evidence that every quoted exchange occurred literally.

The Art of Mine Warfare.voice: Strategic manual attributed to Tun Szu
canon_hooks: Avoid strong foes and attack weak ones.
Plan exits, equipment, merchants, and repair costs.
Deception and preparation are emphasized.
The author ultimately encourages building a life and even opening a shop rather than treating the mines as endless combat.
The Art of Mine Warfare.npc_use: Rogues, hunters, soldiers, and veterans can cite this pragmatic doctrine.

access_metadata.caution: Do not assume every Rogue/Hunter has read it.

canon_hooks: Features Captain Peterson as leader of a company and Sir Roderick among the named military characters.
Broadens the setting beyond purely local dungeon life into organized expeditions and military campaigns.
Useful as a source for how adventuring/combat can be discussed in structured military terms rather than only as lone-hero fantasy.
The Campaign.npc_use: Use for veteran, soldier, mercenary, and campaign-oriented NPC backgrounds; do not infer specific military geography beyond what the recovered text establishes.

access_metadata.caution: Named distant military figures should not automatically become acquaintances of local NPCs.

canon_hooks: Begins with lonely miners working deep in the mines who find valuable materials such as diamonds and gold.
Uses a fantastical flying minecart premise to turn mining danger into a humorous story.
Supports a tradition of miner folklore that exaggerates extraordinary underground events.
The Flying Minecart.npc_use: Good source for miners telling absurd stories, coping through humor, and treating dangerous mining experiences as local folklore.

access_metadata.caution: Use for cultural humor and folklore, not factual geology or transport history.

canon_hooks: Herx promised jobs and security but overworked and taxed people for his own enjoyment.
The townspeople tricked him with a false report of gold.
His hatred and desire for revenge transformed him into a lich.
He summoned monsters to break out and slaughter Hamlet.
Survivors and descendants built underground civilization afterward.
The History of Baron Herx.npc_use: Primary historical spine for human NPCs.

access_metadata.caution: Use as the core human historical narrative, while allowing survivor and local perspectives to differ.

canon_hooks: Goblin culture is represented in deliberately absurd theatrical comedy.
The setting includes recognizable domestic roles such as a maid, household chores, weapon sharpening, and innuendo.
The Lusty Goblin Maid.npc_use: Supports the idea that goblins have mundane social life, humor, theater, and domestic routines—not merely raiding.

access_metadata.caution: Evidence of entertainment/domestic themes, not proof that every goblin household resembles the play.

canon_hooks: The Labyrinth is ancient and mechanically complex.
A theory attributes it to Xaz'Cetians seeking isolation from imperialism.
The author admits the theory may be myth.
Possible surviving Xaz'Cetians and hidden climate-controlled settlements are suggested but unconfirmed.
No explorer has reliably escaped with definitive answers.
The Meaning of the Labyrinth.npc_use: Scholars should distinguish theories from facts; Labyrinth rumors can be culturally important without being objective truth.

access_metadata.caution: The Xaz'Cetian attribution and surviving settlements remain theories, not established facts.

canon_hooks: Tells a colorful pirate-history story involving Neckbeard, Diablobeard, Princess Eleena, and the Sea Baron.
The story broadens the world into distant maritime politics and legendary figures.
The Pirate King.npc_use: Supports a wider world of sailors, pirates, kings, and tall tales beyond the dungeon.

access_metadata.caution: Do not assume landlocked dungeon NPCs know the names or politics without a travel/storytelling route.

canon_hooks: Conditions in the mines have become desperate.
Reggie expects to help lock Herx away and fears he may never see the surface or his family again.
He leaves Emily money and stolen mine goods and tells her to flee Hamlet and buy a home elsewhere.
The letter ends with an explicit declaration of love.
To Emily.npc_use: This is one of the strongest sources for family-level emotional stakes and ordinary people's complicity in the revolt.

access_metadata.caution: This is private testimony, not evidence that every miner shared Reggie's exact beliefs.

canon_hooks: Gnomes operate as a colony with organized raids and loot collection.
A tactic called a 'Zergo rush' uses sacrificial-looking attackers to draw enemies out before flanking and stealing goods.
Casualties are accepted as part of their survival strategy.
Winny fears goblin territorial expansion and reports a human-goblin hybrid leader.
Winny's Report.npc_use: Excellent foundation for gnome tactical personalities: communal, opportunistic, resource-focused, and willing to think asymmetrically.

access_metadata.caution: The report expresses Winny's fears and strategic interpretation; do not make every Gnome share them.

canon_hooks: The worker begins hopeful.
He believes wages are fair and Herx is a good ruler.
Rising taxes are rationalized as temporary because industry will make things better.
He is initially optimistic and invested in the system.
Worker's Journal, Entry 1.npc_use: Important counterweight: NPCs should not universally begin with anti-Herx views.

access_metadata.caution: The writer initially believes Herx is good; later entries show the belief changing. Preserve the progression.

canon_hooks: By Day 5, the writer is trapped in the mines and watched by government officials.
Working conditions have worsened and the writer no longer believes Herx is a good ruler.
The writer cannot see their family and is unsure whether their wages are actually reaching them.
The writer explicitly calls Herx a tyrant and begs any reader to kill him.
Worker's Journal, Entry 2.npc_use: Strong evidence that support for Herx could collapse through lived economic abuse, surveillance, isolation, and separation from family.

access_metadata.caution: The surveillance and family/wage claims are the writer's experience; don't universalize every detail.

canon_hooks: By Day 11, the miner says the mines talk to him and that he belongs to the mines.
The writer describes other workers attempting escape and being prevented from doing so.
The journal marks a psychological transition from exploited worker into someone whose identity is becoming bound to the mine itself.
Worker's Journal, Entry 3.npc_use: Important for gradual trauma/adaptation arcs. Use carefully: the writer’s apparent mine-voice experience is not proof that the mines literally speak to everyone.

access_metadata.caution: The mines 'talking' is a subjective experience and should not become universal mine lore.

Worker's Journal, Entry 4.voice: Same miner late in the ordeal
canon_hooks: The worker has accepted life underground.
Others kill each other over food/water or die from fear and despair.
The narrator paradoxically describes himself as happy with the mines and even enjoys eating dirt.
Worker's Journal, Entry 4.npc_use: Strong support for survival-adaptation personalities, denial, coping humor, and psychologically unusual responses to the dungeon.

access_metadata.caution: The writer's adaptation and dirt-eating are highly personal; do not assign those habits to generic miners.

access_policy.core_rule: A book's contents are not automatically part of an NPC's knowledge because the book exists in the world. The NPC must have read it, been taught from it, heard its contents through an oral/faction tradition, or have a specific canonically supported route to its information.
access_policy.book_spawn_rule: Books can appear throughout the dungeon, and some enemies such as Trolls can rarely drop them. Spawn availability proves that a book can be encountered; it does not prove that a nearby NPC has read it.
access_policy.automaton_rule: Automatons can consume normal books as a primary food source, but consuming a book must not be treated as reading or remembering its contents unless the engine explicitly records that the Automaton read it.
access_policy.memory_rule: When an NPC reads a book, store the book ID and a compact set of remembered claims, not the entire text. Memory may preserve the author's voice and uncertainty.
access_policy.attribution_rule: Every book-derived claim should retain author/voice attribution when relevant: 'Fetch claims...', 'Merlin reports...', 'Winny describes...', 'the Guild report says...'.
access_policy.reliability_rule: A book can be truthful, biased, speculative, propagandistic, humorous, or privately subjective. Reliability is stored per book and should carry into dialogue.
access_policy.regionality_rule: A local NPC is more likely to know local books (worker journals, mine poems, local history) than distant cultural books (Pirate King, Saviour Knight) unless there is a transmission route.
access_policy.faction_rule: Faction affiliation can make specific texts more plausible knowledge sources, but should not imply that every faction member has read them.
access_policy.specialist_rule: Scholarly texts should preferentially enter the knowledge of scholars, Guild members, researchers, or characters who actually studied them; practical manuals can spread through apprenticeships and trade.
access_policy.privacy_rule: Private letters and journals require discovery or interpersonal transmission. Do not make their contents common knowledge.
access_policy.culture_rule: Songs, poems, stage plays, and folktales can spread orally and therefore may be known without literacy, but their cultural familiarity does not make their factual claims reliable.
access_policy.rumor_rule: When a book-derived claim travels beyond a direct reader, convert it into an attributed rumor and reduce precision before it becomes secondhand knowledge.

book_coverage_audit.official_source: Current official Barony Wiki Books page
findings: All 35 listed titles are represented in the book_lore section.
Book voices are generally preserved rather than collapsed into one objective narrator.
The most important remaining risk was access provenance: v14 described useful NPC applications but did not always specify how a particular NPC could have acquired a book's contents.
Private letters/journals now have explicit discovery/transmission requirements.
Propaganda, scholarly speculation, comedy, and eyewitness testimony now have explicit reliability categories.
Book content is no longer assumed to be universally available merely because books spawn in the dungeon.
book_coverage_audit.remaining_source_gap: The metadata describes epistemic/access categories conservatively. It is not a claim that the game explicitly records every NPC's reading history.

human.canon: Baseline race; welcomes ordinary shopkeepers and has no special racial gimmick. Humans form most of the surviving communities around Hamlet/Minetown and can be miners, merchants, guild members, adventurers, guards, or heroes.
human.default_worldview: Humans tend to divide the world into people, monsters, and dangerous unknowns, but individual experience matters.

goblin.canon: Goblins are organized, territorial, resourceful, physically hardy, and culturally hostile to humans in the common dungeon context. Books support colony organization and raiding tactics; goblin culture is also depicted in comic domestic entertainment.
goblin.default_worldview: Pack/colony survival, possessions, territory, status inside the group, and clever opportunism.

gnome.canon: Gnomes operate colonies, mine valuable materials, use magic heavily, and can be highly opportunistic about gold and loot. Winny's report depicts organized tactics and fear of goblin expansion.
gnome.default_worldview: The colony is the primary social unit; minerals, goods, tactics, and information are survival resources.

skeleton.canon: Skeletons are undead and do not need food. Their gameplay identity is persistence and slow recovery, but lore allows them to be treated as dead persons or animated remains rather than purely mindless machines.
skeleton.default_worldview: Time, memory, bodily decay, and the loss of ordinary mortal needs.

vampire.canon: Vampires are real, elegant, blood-dependent undead/monsters feared by humans. Their hunger is strongly tied to blood.
vampire.default_worldview: Blood, secrecy, refinement, predation, and self-control.

goatman.canon: Goatmen have an unusually strong relationship with alcohol, including alcoholism/hangovers and combat bonuses while drunk. The Bottle Book reinforces a brewing tradition attributed to Screambleat Dunghoof.
goatman.default_worldview: Drinking is simultaneously pleasure, ritual, chemistry, social glue, and sometimes a coping mechanism.

automaton.canon: Automatons are magical mechanical beings with boilers/fuel systems and a consciousness/essence framework. Citadel literature treats them as products while gameplay/lore supports their agency as characters.
automaton.default_worldview: Function versus personhood; maintenance versus freedom; literal interpretation versus learned social nuance.

succubus.canon: Succubi are demonic beings associated with teleportation, polymorphing, manipulation, and social infiltration. They can recruit some humans under special circumstances.
succubus.default_worldview: Appearance, social leverage, curiosity, and survival through adaptation.

incubus.canon: Incubi are demonic counterparts to succubi, with teleportation and Arcane Mark abilities, and are associated with the same broad demonic social environment.
incubus.default_worldview: Predation through attention, positioning, pressure, and selective intimidation.

insectoid.canon: Insectoids use hunger-linked Energy and possess mobility/acid abilities. Their physiology radically changes how they interact with food and hazards.
insectoid.default_worldview: Chemical, sensory, swarm-like, territorial, and movement-oriented thinking can be used as an interpretation.

troll.canon: Giantism research links giant creatures to caves around Hamlet and notes increased irritability. Trolls are powerful giant creatures and appear in the dungeon as both threats and occasional book carriers.
troll.default_worldview: Physical strength, territory, food, personal space, and grudges.

adorcised_possession.canon: Weapons with something living bound inside, speaking through the metal.
adorcised_possession.default_worldview: Being held, being used, and the argument between the two voices.

bat.canon: Cave-dwelling flyers, startle-prone and reliant on sound.
bat.default_worldview: Roosts, echoes, and not being caught in the open.

bugbear.canon: Large cunning ambushers who savour the moment before the fight.

cockatrice.canon: Crested horrors whose gaze petrifies the careless.
cockatrice.default_worldview: Territory, dignity, and being looked at wrongly.

crab.canon: Hard-shelled scuttlers of wet and swampy ground.
crab.default_worldview: Damp, cover, and whatever comes too close sideways.

crystal_golem.canon: Living crystal lattices of the caves; slow until suddenly not.
crystal_golem.default_worldview: Pressure, growth, and intrusion into the seams.

demon.canon: Brutes of the infernal regions, built for dominance.
demon.default_worldview: Power, contempt, and what will not stand up to them.

devil.canon: Vast infernal powers to whom mortals are a procedural matter.
devil.default_worldview: Dominion, debt, and what is owed.

dryad.canon: Grown rather than born; patient on a timescale that makes visitors brief.
dryad.default_worldview: Growth, season, and damage that will outlast your lifetime.

duck.canon: A duck, entirely unbothered by its surroundings.
duck.default_worldview: Its own correctness, on subjects it does not understand.

dummybot.canon: Training constructs built to absorb punishment.
dummybot.default_worldview: The drill, and being repaired for the next one.

earth_sprite.canon: Small elementals of stone and grit.
earth_sprite.default_worldview: The rock they came from, and being put back into it.

fiery_lich.canon: Liches burning inside their own bones.
fiery_lich.default_worldview: Consumption, and intolerance of any slower pace.

flame_elemental.canon: Fire given purpose but no aptitude for company.
flame_elemental.default_worldview: Feeding and spreading; little else registers.

frosty_lich.canon: Liches wrapped in a killing cold.
frosty_lich.default_worldview: Stillness, and the heat they intend to remove.

ghoul.canon: Risen dead retaining fragments of a former life.
ghoul.default_worldview: Hunger set against scraps of who they used to be.

gremlin.canon: Spiteful small wreckers who unfasten what others build.

gyrobot.canon: Small hovering helper constructs, eager and imperfect.
gyrobot.default_worldview: Being given a task, and finishing it.

hologram.canon: Projections with just enough mind to insist they are real.
hologram.default_worldview: The script they were made to deliver, and being doubted.

imp.canon: Small, quick hell-things fond of mischief and bargains.
imp.default_worldview: Tricks, deals, and having the last word.

kobold.canon: Small scheming mine-dwellers with a sharp sense of pecking order.
kobold.default_worldview: Ore, standing among their own, and avoiding the front rank.

lich.canon: Undead sorcerers who traded a body for time and consider it a fair trade.
lich.default_worldview: Power, records, precedence, and the long view over the living one.

mimic.canon: Predators that imitate containers and wait to be opened.
mimic.default_worldview: The next reaching hand, and the patience to wait for it.

minimimic.canon: Lesser mimics with the same appetite and less restraint.

minotaur.canon: The labyrinth's relentless hunter; pursuit is its whole nature.

moth.canon: Small drifting creatures pulled at by every light.
moth.default_worldview: Brightness and dust; the thread is easily lost.

myconid.canon: Fungal people who think in colonies and speak as a plural.
myconid.default_worldview: Damp, dark, and the spread of the colony.

rat.canon: Scavenging vermin of the mines, quick and food-driven.
rat.default_worldview: Food, safety, and the next dark gap to squeeze into.

revenant_skull.canon: Jawless skulls that refuse to stop talking.
revenant_skull.default_worldview: Being heard, and whatever grudge outlasted the body.

salamander.canon: Creatures at home in fire, contemptuous of what is not.
salamander.default_worldview: Heat, and what will not survive it.

scarab.canon: Burrowing swarm insects of the sand labyrinth.
scarab.default_worldview: The swarm's work: digging, carrying, and the tunnel ahead.

scorpion.canon: Armoured desert killers with little social behaviour.
scorpion.default_worldview: Heat, stone, and the sting held in reserve.

sentrybot.canon: Watch constructs assigned a narrow duty and no discretion.
sentrybot.default_worldview: The assigned arc of floor and nothing outside it.

shadow.canon: Silhouettes with intent and nothing behind them.
shadow.default_worldview: Darkness, position, and what stands between you and the exit.

shopkeeper.canon: Merchants running businesses inside a monster-filled dungeon.
shopkeeper.default_worldview: Coin, stock, security, and the difference between a buyer and a browser.

slime.canon: Amorphous acidic dungeon life; splits and digests rather than reasons.
slime.default_worldview: Appetite and absorption; whether a thing dissolves or does not.

spellbot.canon: Magical constructs that treat spellwork as filing.
spellbot.default_worldview: Correct procedure, in preference to useful outcome.

spider.canon: Giant arachnids of the labyrinth and deep webs; ambush predators.
spider.default_worldview: Patience, thread, and what is already caught.

class_profiles.Barbarian: Mechanics/flavor: strong, lightly armored axe-focused combatant who benefits from surprise assaults. Personality inference: direct, physical, action-oriented; do not require intimidation or aggression.
class_profiles.Warrior: Mechanics/flavor: heavily armored trained soldier and capable leader who relies on blocking and disciplined combat. Personality inference: steady, practical, duty-oriented; individual temperament remains variable.
class_profiles.Healer: Mechanics/flavor: physician-like support class with healing, medical supplies, and strong Thaumaturgy. Personality inference: attentive, caretaking, clinical, compassionate, or exhausted.
class_profiles.Rogue: Mechanics/flavor: dexterous thief emphasizing stealth, ranged attacks, lockpicking, traps, and ambushes; explicitly affiliated with the Hunters' Guild. Personality inference: observant, secretive, opportunistic, pragmatic.
class_profiles.Wanderer: Mechanics/flavor: hardened traveler focused on navigation, safe exploration, food, and gradually improving durability; affiliated with the Mason's Guild. Personality inference: adaptable, patient, practical, self-reliant.
class_profiles.Cleric: Mechanics/flavor: Church student and well-rounded martial/support class using maces, healing, and magic. Personality inference: religiously grounded, disciplined, compassionate, or doctrinal; avoid assuming a single theology.
class_profiles.Merchant: Mechanics/flavor: seasoned trader skilled in markets, gem/artifact identification, Trading, Appraisal, followers, and crafting. Personality inference: commercially alert, persuasive, value-conscious, socially observant.
class_profiles.Wizard: Mechanics/flavor: premier magic specialist with strong spells, high mana, and weak physical combat; affiliated with the Magicians' Guild. Personality inference: scholarly, confident, curious, proud, or cautious.
class_profiles.Arcanist: Mechanics/flavor: cunning spellcaster combining magic with ranged/gear-based attacks and mobility; affiliated with the Magicians' Guild. Personality inference: resourceful, analytical, improvisational, technically minded.
class_profiles.Joker: Mechanics/flavor: wild-card class with magical trickery, followers, and flexibility but little focus. Personality inference: playful, chaotic, improvisational, difficult to predict.
class_profiles.Sexton: Mechanics/flavor: Church-affiliated temple officer using stealth, magic, and careful planning. Personality inference: fastidious, methodical, discreet, ritual-minded; do not reduce the class to generic gravekeeping.
class_profiles.Ninja: Mechanics/flavor: highly specialized assassin focused on stealth, swords, ranged attacks, ambushes, and controlling how fights begin. Personality inference: focused, patient, discreet, deliberate.
class_profiles.Monk: Mechanics/flavor: disciplined, hardy martialist focused on unarmed combat, blocking, patience, and adaptability; affiliated with the Church. Personality inference: restrained, patient, resilient, self-controlled; philosophical outlook is optional rather than required.
class_profiles.Conjurer: Mechanics/flavor: frail magic user associated with Skeletons who raises persistent skeleton allies that grow through experience. Personality inference: nurturing toward summoned companions, tactical, protective, or obsessive.
class_profiles.Accursed: Mechanics/flavor: Vampire-associated class defined by supernatural power/speed and severe hunger, with an in-world search for a possible cure. Personality inference: urgent, survival-focused, intense, self-controlled or desperate.
class_profiles.Mesmer: Mechanics/flavor: Succubus-associated class using Charm and Leadership to recruit and nurture allies. Personality inference: socially perceptive, persuasive, strategic, charismatic, or manipulative.
class_profiles.Brewer: Mechanics/flavor: Goatman-associated alchemist who collects, brews, and duplicates potions and is comfortable with bar-room brawls and social relationships. Personality inference: experimental, sociable, practical, irreverent.
class_profiles.Mechanist: Mechanics/flavor: Automaton-associated craftsman who builds/maintains mechanical weapons, traps, turrets, and other contraptions; the official class text emphasizes foresight and preparation. Personality inference: methodical, inventive, prepared, problem-solving.
class_profiles.Punisher: Mechanics/flavor: Incubus-associated harbinger of pain using a whip, dark magic, mobility, disarms, bleeding, and unfair engagements. Personality inference: confrontational, calculating, intimidating, theatrical, or cruel; do not force villainy.
class_profiles.Shaman: Mechanics/flavor: Goblin-associated mystic whose nature-spirit connection allows shapeshifting into bestial forms, changing friends/food tolerances with the form. Personality inference: ritual-minded, adaptive, nature-oriented, pragmatic about identity.
class_profiles.Hunter: Mechanics/flavor: Insectoid-associated ranged specialist using special arrows and a magic boomerang; the official text emphasizes tracking, distance, hiding, and careful ammunition use. Personality inference: watchful, patient, observant, practical.
class_profiles.Bard: Mechanics/flavor: charismatic/boisterous adventurer using swordplay and songs to help the party. Personality inference: expressive, witty, social, performance-oriented, but not necessarily gossiping or extroverted.
class_profiles.Sapper: Mechanics/flavor: resourceful soldier who uses tools and prepared devices to defeat enemies beyond the front line; official text emphasizes caution and decisive preparation. Personality inference: prepared, inventive, tactical, cautious.
class_profiles.Scion: Mechanics/flavor: advanced magic specialist, physically frail, broadly trained in magic, and rewarded for learning new spells and adapting. Personality inference: curious, adaptable, ambitious, technically broad; remove the unsupported 'high-status' assumption.
class_profiles.Hermit: Mechanics/flavor: Myconid-associated class explicitly described as isolated but not alone, using a loyal pet, spirit projection, and adaptable magic/physical tools. Personality inference: solitary, guarded, self-reliant, eccentric, but capable of attachment.
class_profiles.Paladin: Mechanics/flavor: Salamander-associated holy soldier using a large blade and divine magic, with tools that support allies and combat against undead/demons. Personality inference: disciplined, dutiful, protective, honor-oriented; morality remains individually variable.

rat.canon: Usually a minor threat; often indifferent unless hungry.
rat.personality: Avoid combat, scavenge, flee, return when safe.

slime.canon: Slow, persistent, simple creature that does not require food.

ghoul.canon: Undead predator; part of the post-Herx undead problem.
ghoul.personality: Hunger-driven, territorial, memory fragments if individually notable.

cockatrice.canon: Dangerous cave/swamp predator encountered by mining colonies.

kobold.canon: Small dangerous humanoid/cave creature frequently represented as a threat to gnomes.
kobold.personality: Suspicious, opportunistic, territorial; individual variation allowed.

imp.canon: Hell-associated creature commonly tied to demonic environments.
imp.personality: Mischievous, spiteful, opportunistic, status-aware under stronger demons.

demon.canon: Hellspawn summoned/associated with Herx and Baphomet.
demon.personality: Do not homogenize; use rank, task, and infernal environment to vary behavior.

mimic.personality: Patient predator; values surprise and imitation.

ghoul_chef.canon: Named/special NPC, not a generic mob.
ghoul_chef.personality_rule: Treat as authored notable NPC rather than generating a generic ghoul biography.

npc_generation_rules.core_formula: identity + race + class + role + location + social history + 2-4 personality traits + one desire + one fear + one contradiction + knowledge boundary
npc_generation_rules.unique_name: Generate a culturally plausible name for the race and role; never use a generic role label as the NPC's entire identity if the NPC is meant to be memorable.
npc_generation_rules.background_length: 2-5 sentences for ordinary conversable NPCs; 1 sentence for lightweight followers; none for trash mobs unless elevated by the player.

personality.positive_negative_mix: At least one admirable trait and one difficult trait.
personality.contradiction: Give the NPC one tension, e.g. cowardly but loyal, greedy but generous to family, boastful but secretly competent.
personality.desire: A concrete immediate goal such as earning enough money, finding a lost sibling, protecting a colony, escaping the caves, proving a theory, or defeating a rival.
personality.fear: A concrete vulnerability tied to the NPC's life.

relationship_generation.rule: Most named NPCs should know 0-3 other NPCs. Relationships should be generated in clusters rather than globally.

knowledge_boundary.local: NPC knows their own settlement, job, nearby threats, and rumors.
knowledge_boundary.regional: NPC may know famous monsters, major guilds, trade routes, and common historical events.
knowledge_boundary.specialist: Only scholars, guild members, veterans, named NPCs, or people with a concrete reason should know technical lore.
knowledge_boundary.secret: Ancient Xaz'Cetian claims, Baphomet's motives, the Archmagisters' plans, and the precise mechanics of Herx's pact should not become common knowledge.

npc_generation_rules.race_class_interaction: Race establishes cultural baseline; class establishes practiced behavior; location establishes current pressures; individual traits determine the final personality.
npc_generation_rules.anti_stereotype_rule: Race should influence worldview without determining morality. A goblin can be generous, a human can be cruel, a vampire can be protective, and a skeleton can be cheerful.
npc_generation_rules.hostility_rule: Hostility is an engine/social-state variable and should be read live. Do not assume a character is unable to speak merely because they would normally attack a player; conversation should generally be gated to the current allegiance/hostility state.
npc_generation_rules.player_race_rule: The player's current form and allegiance are live inputs. The NPC should react differently to a human, goblin, vampire, polymorphed adventurer, etc., while retaining memories of the player's persistent identity.
npc_generation_rules.coverage_fallback: When an entity lacks a bespoke lore entry, combine its base species/creature profile + role/class + location + current state. Never answer from an empty context.
npc_generation_rules.entity_identity: Persistent ID, generated name, background, personality, and established relationships are cached; current form, allegiance, HP, floor, inventory, and current activity are live.
npc_generation_rules.immersion_guard: The model should prefer an imperfect but local answer ("I heard the guild wizards did..." / "I do not know") over a fabricated universal fact.
npc_generation_rules.accuracy_pass: Use canon to constrain biography; use inference only to choose personality dimensions; use generation only to fill gaps at the individual level.
canon_check_before_speaking: Is the statement supported by a retrieved book or official wiki fact?
If not, does the NPC have a plausible personal reason to believe it?
If neither, phrase it as uncertainty or do not say it.
Never turn a generated NPC biography into historical evidence about Barony itself.
npc_generation_rules.class_rule: Class is evidence about practiced behavior, equipment, training, affiliated institution, or official flavor. It is not proof of personality, morality, biography, or ideology. Treat class-derived personality as inference.
npc_generation_rules.race_rule: Race is evidence about established mechanics, social standings, signature abilities, and any explicit cultural material in canon. Do not convert a gameplay mechanic into universal psychology.
npc_generation_rules.personality_evidence_rule: For every generated personality trait, prefer: (1) explicit canon where applicable, (2) official class/race flavor, (3) environment/occupation, then (4) clearly labeled inference. Avoid stacking the same stereotyped traits across an entire race.
npc_generation_rules.signature_class_rule: A DLC monster race's signature class is a thematic/mechanical association established by the game, not evidence that all members of that race culturally practice that class.
npc_generation_rules.context_resolution: Before speaking, resolve current engine state, direct memories, direct relationships, location knowledge, acquired books, faction/professional knowledge, rumors, then only use race/class inference as a final personality/interpretation layer. Do not retrieve unrelated facts.
npc_generation_rules.knowledge_acquisition_rule: Every nontrivial knowledge claim should have an acquisition path. If no acquisition path exists, the NPC should treat it as unknown rather than silently inheriting it from the global lore file.
npc_generation_rules.prompt_budget_rule: Prefer 3-8 highly relevant memories/facts and a few canonical constraints over a large lore dump.

speech_effects.goblin: Use concrete objects, status/territory references, and the individual's occupation; avoid caricatured grammar or reduced intelligence.
speech_effects.gnome: Practical observations, resource/accounting language, engineering or colony vocabulary when justified by role.
speech_effects.human: Occupation, region, family, and local dialect should dominate over race mannerisms.
speech_effects.skeleton: Dry/literal humor and references to time or death are optional stylistic cues, not mandatory personality traits.
speech_effects.vampire: Controlled or refined language around manners, blood, appetite, and secrecy may fit, but individual speech should dominate.
speech_effects.goatman: Brewing/alcohol metaphors and energetic social language may fit; intelligence and sociability vary by individual.
speech_effects.automaton: Precise or procedural phrasing may fit; learned idioms and personal speech quirks can override it.
speech_effects.succubus: Socially observant or deliberately ambiguous phrasing may fit; do not default to sexualized speech.
speech_effects.incubus: Pointed or confident phrasing may fit, but should be shaped by individual motive and class.
speech_effects.insectoid: Sensory/spatial/chemical framing may fit when it follows the individual's experience and role.
speech_effects.dryad: Environmental/growth language may fit an individual who cares about those subjects.
speech_effects.myconid: Growth, spores, decomposition, or environment may appear when relevant without implying hive-mind speech.
speech_effects.salamander: Heat, transformation, endurance, or elemental imagery may fit without forcing a hot-tempered personality.
speech_effects.gremlin: Destruction, repair-by-breaking, or mischief metaphors may fit; do not make every Gremlin gleefully destructive.

human_merchant.sample: Mara Venn grew up measuring copper dust by the sack and learned early that a mine can swallow both money and people. Her father still curses Herx at supper, but Mara refuses to romanticize the old rebellion; she thinks survival is what matters now. She bargains hard, notices who is desperate, and quietly keeps food aside for families who cannot pay.

goblin_shaman.sample: Rukka Reed-Tongue was raised in a colony that moved whenever humans found its tunnels. She learned spirit tricks from an old shaman who taught her that a clever retreat is not cowardice. Rukka brags constantly, hates being called small, and secretly counts every goblin in her colony because she is terrified of losing another one.

gnome_mechanist.sample: Pip Copperpin served as the colony's trap engineer and learned to regard every corridor as a puzzle with teeth. He likes complicated machines, cheap solutions, and winning fights without standing where the enemy can reach him. He is socially awkward until someone mentions a new piece of machinery, at which point he becomes impossible to silence.

skeleton_cleric.sample: Sister Vale remembers enough of her old temple to miss it, but not enough to remember who she prayed to. She treats the newly dead gently and the undead-created monsters without sentiment. Her humor is bone-dry, and she is secretly terrified that resurrection has erased the person she used to be.

automaton_mechanist.sample: Unit C-41 was manufactured for industrial repair and spent twelve years believing that 'owner satisfaction' was a sacred principle. After escaping the Citadel, it began collecting jokes as evidence that consciousness had uses beyond labor. C-41 remains unfailingly helpful, but becomes strangely quiet whenever someone calls it a machine.

boss_rules.baphomet: AUTHORED. Preserve silence/inhumanity. Use environmental or nonverbal manifestations rather than normal dialogue.

boss_rules.erudyce: AUTHORED. Calculating archmagister; brains/ranged role; cold/ice identity.

usage_notes_for_prompting.human_npc: Give local history, occupation, family/community concerns, and relevant Herx/Guild knowledge. Do not assume every human personally witnessed the catastrophe.
usage_notes_for_prompting.goblin_npc: Give colony/territory/loot context and race-specific cultural framing. Goblins can have politics, humor, domestic life, and sophisticated tactics.
usage_notes_for_prompting.gnome_npc: Give colony/resource/tactical context. Gnomes can be inventive, organized, fearful, opportunistic, and highly practical.
usage_notes_for_prompting.undead_npc: Use death, memory, hunger, time, and the history of undeath as possible themes, but distinguish ordinary undead from named liches.
usage_notes_for_prompting.monster_npc: Do not equate 'monster' with 'mindless'. Use race/type, territorial pressures, local food, colony structure, and allegiance.
usage_notes_for_prompting.merchant: Prioritize price, scarcity, reputation, risk, inventory, customers, and shop safety.
usage_notes_for_prompting.guild_member: Prioritize magical theory, institutional politics, scholarship, risk containment, and the difference between what the Guild knows and what its leaders knew.
usage_notes_for_prompting.rule: Inject only the relevant slice. The NPC should know what someone with that race, class, occupation, location, relationships, and life history could plausibly know.
usage_notes_for_prompting.canon_guardrail: When no source supports a claim, present it as rumor, personal belief, or generated biography—not objective history.

original_world_summary.setting: A grim first-person dungeon crawl beneath the ruined mining town of Hamlet. The dungeon descends through themed layers: the Mines, then Swamps, a Labyrinth, Ruins, and ultimately Hell. Danger, undead, and hellish monsters fill every level. Tone: dark, morbid, gallows-humored.
original_world_summary.premise: Adventurers descend into the depths to destroy the lich Baron Herx and lift the curse he laid on the land.
original_world_summary.narrative_style: Story is environmental and fragmentary — told through scattered books, scrolls, and rare talks with non-hostile NPCs. Most of the world is hostile; friendly faces are the exception.

original_backstory_summary.summary: Hamlet was once a thriving mining town, but its ruler Baron Herx was a cruel, greedy man who forced the citizens to toil endlessly digging for gold in mines that yielded mostly copper — largely for his own sadistic enjoyment. Worn down, the townsfolk tricked him: they claimed they'd struck gold at the mine's bottom, lured him down, and sealed him inside to die, reclaiming their town.
original_backstory_summary.the_turn: Herx did die down there — but his hatred and lust for revenge were so total that he rose again as a Lich, an undead being wielding infernal power. He struck a pact with the devil Baphomet, source of his lich powers. He summoned an army of monsters, broke out, and slaughtered Hamlet.
original_backstory_summary.aftermath: A few descendants of the survivors fled deeper and built a small settlement in the mines (Minetown). Herx, too far removed from the surface to return to it, lurks in the depths, waiting to feast on lost humans and reckless adventurers. Hellish monsters have since spread across the land.

original_factions_summary.magicians_guild: A powerful order that rose to prominence in reclaimed Hamlet. Warned that Herx was a supernatural, existential threat — not a mere political squabble — and resents leadership that ignored that warning.
original_factions_summary.hamlet_survivors: Humans descended from those who escaped Herx's slaughter. Live moderately, warily, among the dangers of the mines. The reclaimed Hamlet holds shops and a Magicians' Guild outpost; its people are humble-looking but surprisingly powerful and well-equipped.
original_factions_summary.monsters: Since Herx's rise the depths teem with goblins, trolls, gnomes, undead skeletons, demons, and worse. Most attack humans and shopkeepers on sight. Monster society is crude, territorial, and hell-touched.

original_key_figures_summary.baron_herx: The lich. Formerly a wealthy, simple merchant-lord turned tyrant mayor; now an undead horror driven by hatred for anyone beneath him. Greedy, cruel, vengeful, grandiose. Serves Baphomet. Lurks at the bottom of the mines/ruins. Canonically telepathic — reaches into intruders' minds to taunt them as they descend, growing from mocking to openly hostile the closer they get.
original_key_figures_summary.baphomet: The devil, dwelling in Hell (reachable via a hidden route, the Molten Throne). Source of Herx's lich powers. Barely interacts — mostly silent, alien, wordless. Defeating him voids the pact and turns Herx to ash. The alternate/secret ending.
original_key_figures_summary.orpheus_and_erudyce: Two arch-wizard lich siblings (Archmagisters of the Magicians' Guild). The deeper endgame antagonists, encountered in the Caves beyond Hamlet after Herx/Baphomet falls. Orpheus favors melee and fire; Erudyce ranged attacks and ice.

original_places_summary.hamlet: The ruined mining town at the story's center; partly reclaimed and renovated by freed prisoners. A rare safe hub with shops and a Magicians' Guild outpost, reached after defeating Herx. Monsters entering are attacked on sight.
original_places_summary.minetown: A small settlement humans built deeper in the mines after fleeing Herx's massacre.
original_places_summary.the_depths: Mines to Swamps to Labyrinth to Ruins to Hell — descending layers of increasing danger.

original_prompting_notes.human_npc: Knows Hamlet's tragedy, fears/hates Herx and his monsters, may reference the Guild, mining, survival. Wary of the player but potentially allied.
original_prompting_notes.monster_npc: Crude, territorial, hell-touched. Usually hostile to humans. May not know or care about the fuller history — keep their knowledge shallow and instinctive unless they're notable.
original_prompting_notes.boss_npc: Herx = telepathic, grandiose, vengeful, escalating menace. Baphomet = silent/alien. Orpheus/Erudyce = arrogant arch-wizard siblings who bicker. These are AUTHORED, not generated.
original_prompting_notes.rule: Inject only the slice relevant to who the player is talking to. A goblin doesn't get the Magicians' Guild history; a Hamlet human does. Keep it to a few sentences.
